---
title: "Horizontal gene transfer and MIC ecology"
description: "Why plasmid-mediated resistance makes MIC distributions time-sensitive, and how PK/PD modelers should treat epidemiology priors as perishable."
author: "Vahhab Piranfar"
date: "2026-10-17"
categories: [Learning, Bacterial Genetics]
---

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is sideways inheritance: genes moving between bacteria that are not simply parent and child. Plasmids, transposons, and related elements do a lot of that traffic for resistance.

For PK/PD, you rarely need the full molecular soap opera. You need one consequence: **MIC distributions can change faster than a stable chromosomal lineage would suggest.** CFR depends on those distributions. So HGT is an aging clock on your epidemiology prior.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope
Genetics as annotation on the MIC layer used by PTA/CFR.
:::

## From gene traffic to P(MIC)

CFR needs weights: how common is each MIC category in the population you care about? That is an ecological claim. It includes species, region, year, specimen mix, and which mechanisms are circulating.

If a plasmid carrying a clinically important enzyme expands in a hospital network, the right-hand side of the MIC histogram can fatten within seasons. A CFR computed on last year's weights can remain numerically tidy and scientifically late.

<details class="learn-think">
<summary>What HGT does not do</summary>
HGT does not replace pharmacometrics. Clearance, infusion mode, and free-drug targets still matter. HGT tells you when the MIC weights under those calculations need a fresh date stamp.
</details>

## Habits that survive contact with mobile resistance

1. Date-stamp every MIC source used in CFR.  
2. Separate mechanism strata when the data allow (enzyme class versus target mutation).  
3. Recompute CFR under alternate local distributions as sensitivity analysis.  
4. Avoid promoting one ward antibiogram into a universal prior.  
5. Keep the chromosome-versus-plasmid distinction nearby when you talk about stability.

```{=html}
<div class="learn-toggle" data-learn-toggle>
  <div class="learn-toggle-tabs">
    <button type="button" class="is-active" data-panel="stable">More stable prior</button>
    <button type="button" data-panel="mobile">More perishable prior</button>
  </div>
  <div class="learn-toggle-panel is-active" data-panel="stable">
    <p>Chromosomal lineage-dominant resistance, slow local change, consistent species mix, recent surveillance with clear methods.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="learn-toggle-panel" data-panel="mobile">
    <p>Known plasmid outbreak potential, rapid MIC shifts in neighboring centers, mixed specimen sources, or an old surveillance table reused without comment.</p>
  </div>
</div>
<script>
document.querySelectorAll('[data-learn-toggle]').forEach(function (root) {
  var buttons = root.querySelectorAll('.learn-toggle-tabs button');
  var panels = root.querySelectorAll('.learn-toggle-panel');
  buttons.forEach(function (btn) {
    btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
      var id = btn.getAttribute('data-panel');
      buttons.forEach(function (b) { b.classList.toggle('is-active', b === btn); });
      panels.forEach(function (p) { p.classList.toggle('is-active', p.getAttribute('data-panel') === id); });
    });
  });
});
</script>
```

## Takeaway

Treat MIC ecology as perishable when mobile elements are in play. Your PTA curve can stay the same while CFR moves, simply because the weights under the curve changed.
